name: Punjab
summary: The north-western wheat belt. Food is hearty and dairy-rich, with tandoor-baked breads, ghee, paneer and slow-cooked gravies.

name: Karnataka
summary: A south-western state with a strong tradition of fermented rice-and-lentil batters. The Udupi temple-town kitchens are famous for vegetarian cooking.

name: West Bengal
summary: A river-delta region where rice and freshwater fish anchor meals. Mustard in oil, paste and seed form is a defining flavour, and sweets are a major craft.

name: Gujarat
summary: A largely vegetarian western state. Meals balance sweet, salty and tangy notes, and gram-flour snacks (farsan) are a specialty.

name: Campania
summary: The region around Naples. Volcanic soil produces prized tomatoes, and buffalo mozzarella and pizza are its best-known exports.

name: Emilia-Romagna
summary: A rich agricultural region in the north. Egg pasta, cured pork, Parmigiano Reggiano and slow-simmered meat sauces define it.

name: Sicily
summary: A Mediterranean island shaped by Greek, Arab, Norman and Spanish rule. Rice, saffron, citrus, almonds and street food are all part of it.

name: Lombardy
summary: A northern region centred on Milan. Butter, rice from the Po valley and braised meats take the place of the olive oil used further south.

name: Oaxaca
summary: A southern state with strong indigenous traditions. It is known as the land of seven moles, along with chocolate, mezcal and tlayudas.

name: Yucatan
summary: A peninsula with Maya roots. Cooking uses achiote, sour orange, habanero and pit or banana-leaf techniques.

name: Puebla
summary: A central highland state with a colonial convent-kitchen heritage. It is the home of mole poblano and chiles en nogada.

name: Veracruz
summary: The Gulf coast state and main historical port. Seafood, tomatoes, olives and capers show the Spanish influence, alongside African and Caribbean flavours.

name: Fes
summary: One of the imperial cities, long regarded as a centre of refined urban cooking. Its kitchens are associated with elaborate pastries, sweet-and-savoury combinations and dishes made for weddings and feasts.

name: Marrakech
summary: A southern imperial city and market hub where Amazigh and Arab traditions meet. It is known for slow-baked meat dishes, dried fruit and nuts, and the busy food stalls of its main square.

name: Tangier and the north
summary: The Mediterranean and Rif north, where Andalusian and Spanish influence is strongest. Cooks use more olive oil and fresh herbs, and fish, seafood and vegetable dishes feature widely.

name: Atlantic coast
summary: The long western coastline from Rabat and Casablanca to Essaouira and Safi. Fresh sardines and other fish, grilled or baked with chermoula, are central, and ports are known for simple seafood restaurants.

name: Sahara and the south
summary: Oasis, Atlas and desert country where dates, barley, goat and camel, and argan oil from the south-west are important. Cooking is simple and built for dry, hot conditions.

name: Amhara
summary: The northern and central highlands, where teff injera and spicy wat are everyday food. Orthodox fasting is widely observed, so vegan stews and fasting platters are common alongside festival meat dishes.

name: Oromia
summary: The largest region, spanning highlands and lowlands, and the home of much of the country's coffee. Cooking includes dairy, butter, maize and sorghum alongside injera, and the coffee ceremony is a central social ritual.

name: Tigray
summary: The northern region of the Tigrayan people, whose cooking is close to Eritrean highland food. Chilli-rich stews and shiro, a smooth chickpea-based stew, are staples, especially on fasting days.

name: Southern Ethiopia
summary: The south, formerly grouped as the Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples' Region and now divided, is home to many peoples. Enset (false banana) is a staple in the south-central highlands, and dishes such as Gurage kitfo, cabbage and collards, and fresh cheese are characteristic.

name: Cairo and the Nile Delta
summary: The fertile delta and the capital form the core of Egyptian home and street cooking. Rice, fava beans, lentils and green vegetables dominate, and stuffed vegetables and molokhia are typical of the area.

name: Alexandria and the Mediterranean coast
summary: Egypt's northern coast, with Alexandria as its main port. Fish and seafood are central, cooked with cumin, garlic, tomato and olive oil, and the city's cosmopolitan history shows in its restaurants.

name: Upper Egypt and Nubia
summary: The Nile valley south of Cairo and the Nubian region around Aswan. Dates, wheat, lentils and slow-cooked meat dishes are important, and cooking is typically hearty and less reliant on seafood.

name: Sinai
summary: A desert and coastal peninsula where Bedouin cooking centres on bread baked on hot stones or a convex griddle, lamb or goat, rice and dates. Red Sea and Mediterranean fish are eaten along the coasts.

name: Yoruba south-west
summary: The south-western homeland of the Yoruba, including Lagos, Ibadan and Ogun. Cooking centres on beans, ground peppers, palm and vegetable oil, and pounded yam with green soups; steamed and fried bean snacks are signatures.

name: Igbo south-east
summary: The south-eastern homeland of the Igbo. Yam holds a near-sacred place in the diet, and soups are thickened with ground seeds and leaves and finished with palm oil.

name: Hausa north
summary: The savannah north, home of the Hausa and Fulani. Millet, sorghum and rice are staples, cattle supply milk and meat, and grilled meats with dry spice rubs are a speciality.

name: Niger Delta (South-South)
summary: The creeks and coast of the Niger Delta, home to Urhobo, Ijaw, Efik and other peoples. Fish and shellfish are abundant, and soups are built on palm fruit and fresh or smoked seafood.

name: Cape Malay (Western Cape)
summary: The cooking of the Cape Malay community of Cape Town, shaped by Indonesian, Indian and Dutch influences. Dishes balance warm spices with fruit and sweetness, and baking for religious holidays is a strong tradition.

name: Nguni (Zulu and Xhosa)
summary: The eastern and south-eastern homelands of the Zulu, Xhosa and related Nguni peoples. Maize in the form of porridge and samp, beans, and soured milk are staples, with meat saved for gatherings and ceremonies.

name: Afrikaner
summary: The Dutch-descended farming tradition, centred on meat, sausage, cured and dried meats, and pot cooking over open fires, with sweet baked puddings and fried dough.

name: Durban Indian-South-African
summary: KwaZulu-Natal's Indian-South-African communities, descended largely from indentured labourers, have made Durban a curry city. Chilli-hot, tomato-based curries with lamb, chicken and beans are served in bread, with rice or roti.

name: Highveld and Johannesburg
summary: The inland plateau around Johannesburg and Gauteng, where migrant workers and city dwellers from many communities have made a mixed urban cuisine of maize porridge, braaied meat and spicy relishes.

name: Maharashtra
summary: The western state around Mumbai and Pune. Cooking ranges from everyday street snacks of the cities to spicy, peanut and coconut based home food, with Konkan coastal cooking in the west.

name: Kerala
summary: The south-western coastal state, where coconut, black pepper, curry leaves and tamarind-like souring agents flavour fish, vegetables and rice dishes. Its long spice-trade history shows in its food.

name: Rajasthan
summary: A dry north-western state whose cooking developed around scarce water and fresh vegetables. Lentils, wheat, gram flour, ghee and dried spices are central.

name: Hyderabad and Telangana
summary: The Deccan plateau city of Hyderabad developed a courtly cuisine blending Mughal and local Telugu cooking, known for biryani, slow-cooked meats and rich gravies.

name: Kashmir
summary: The Himalayan valley in the far north. Kashmiri food, with a notable meat tradition, uses dried and ground spices such as fennel and ginger more than fresh onion and garlic in some dishes, and rich red colour from local chilli.

name: Sichuan
summary: The south-western basin province, famous for bold chilli heat paired with the numbing tingle of Sichuan pepper, fermented bean pastes and pickles.

name: Guangdong
summary: The southern coastal province around Guangzhou and Hong Kong. Cantonese cooking prizes fresh ingredients, light seasoning, steaming, roasting and dim sum.

name: Zhejiang
summary: An eastern coastal province in the lower Yangtze region. Cooking favours fresh river and sea produce, rice wine and soy-braising, with a gently sweet balance.

name: Northern China
summary: The wheat-growing north, including Beijing and Shandong. Dumplings, noodles and steamed breads replace rice as the main staple, with garlic, vinegar and braised or roasted meats.

name: Xinjiang
summary: The far north-western region. Uyghur and other Central Asian communities cook lamb, cumin, chilli, flatbreads and rice dishes, with grilled skewers a familiar street food.

name: Hokkaido
summary: The cold northern island with extensive dairy farming, seafood and potatoes. Lamb grilling and hearty hot pots suit the climate.

name: Kanto
summary: The region around Tokyo. Seasoning leans on dark soy sauce, and the old Edo food culture left a legacy of street snacks, soba and sushi.

name: Kansai
summary: The region around Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe. Osaka has a famous casual food culture, called the kitchen of the nation in older accounts, and Kansai cooks favour lighter soy sauce and kombu-based dashi.

name: Kyushu
summary: The south-western island, where cooking is generally richer and sweeter. Pork-bone broths, sweet soy seasoning and seafood are prominent.

name: Okinawa
summary: The southern island chain with its own food culture. Pork, tofu, bitter melon and sweet potato are common, and the cooking blends Japanese, Chinese and Southeast Asian influences.

name: Central Thailand
summary: The Chao Phraya river plain and Bangkok. Rice farming, canals and the royal court shaped a cuisine of refined coconut-milk curries, soups and stir-fries.

name: Northern Thailand
summary: Cool highlands centred on Chiang Mai, historically the Lanna kingdom. Sticky rice, grilled pork, bitter herbs and mildly spiced dips, with influences from Myanmar and Yunnan.

name: Isan (North-East)
summary: The dry north-eastern plateau, culturally close to Laos. Sticky rice is the staple, with grilled meats, pounded salads and fermented fish seasonings.

name: Southern Thailand
summary: A peninsula between two seas, with seafood, fresh turmeric and very hot curries, and a strong Malay and Muslim influence.

name: Northern Vietnam
summary: The Red River Delta and Hanoi. A cooler, more restrained style with noodle soups, grilled meats and subtle seasoning that reflects Chinese influence.

name: Central Vietnam
summary: A narrow coastal strip, including Hue and Hoi An. Dishes are spicier and saltier, with small portions inspired by the imperial court and fermented shrimp.

name: Southern Vietnam
summary: The Mekong Delta and Saigon. A warm, fertile region where food is sweeter, richer in coconut and generous with fresh herbs and fruit.

name: Tuscany
summary: Central Italian region with a frugal, bean-and-bread tradition. Olive oil, beans, kale, bread without salt and simple grilled meats define it.

name: Lazio
summary: The region around Rome, known for pasta with cured pork, pecorino and black pepper, and for offal and vegetable dishes.

name: Puglia
summary: The heel of Italy's boot, with hot dry summers, durum wheat and a food culture built on vegetables, olive oil and handmade pasta.

name: Veneto
summary: A north-eastern region centred on Venice and Verona, with rice, polenta, lagoon fish and festive baking.

name: Alsace
summary: Eastern region on the German border, with a cuisine of pork, sauerkraut, riesling and tarts that reflects centuries of mixed French and German influence.

name: Provence
summary: Mediterranean south-east, where olive oil, garlic, tomatoes, aubergine, herbs and fish from the sea shape the food.

name: Brittany
summary: North-western peninsula known for buckwheat galettes, salted butter, seafood and cider.

name: Burgundy
summary: Eastern-central region famous for its wines, mustard and slow-braised dishes cooked in wine.

name: South-West France
summary: A large area of Languedoc and Gascony with rich, rustic food: duck and goose preserved in their fat, white beans, sausages and garlic.

name: Bavaria
summary: The large southern state, with a hearty beer-garden food culture of pork roasts, sausages, pretzels and dumplings, and Franconian baking.

name: Swabia
summary: South-western region known for hand-made noodles and filled pasta such as spätzle and Maultaschen, plus lentil dishes and alpine cheese.

name: Rhineland
summary: The western Rhine area, where cooking leans on pork, beef braised in wine and vinegar, and sweet-and-sour flavours.

name: Saxony
summary: East German state with a strong baking tradition, famous for Christmas stollen from Dresden, plus potato dishes.

name: Basque Country
summary: A green, Atlantic region with a strong food culture centred on fish, salt cod, peppers and cider. Cooking societies and pintxo bars in towns such as San Sebastián are part of daily life.

name: Catalonia
summary: A Mediterranean region mixing sea and mountain cooking, with bread, tomatoes, olive oil, sauces such as romesco and all-i-oli, and a love of combining meat with fruit or seafood.

name: Andalusia
summary: The hot south, with olive groves, sherry wines and a long Arab-era legacy visible in fried sweets, almonds and spices. Cold soups, fried fish and tapas culture are signatures.

name: Galicia
summary: The rainy north-west Atlantic corner, famous for seafood, octopus, potatoes, paprika and pies. Its produce is among the most prized fish and shellfish in Spain.

name: Valencia
summary: A rice-growing coastal region around the Albufera lagoon and its irrigated orchards. Rice dishes cooked over open flames, citrus and market vegetables define the cooking.

name: Crete
summary: Greece's largest island, with a cuisine closely tied to olive oil, wild greens, fresh cheeses and barley rusks. It is often cited in studies of the traditional Mediterranean diet.

name: Macedonia
summary: The northern region around Thessaloniki, with Balkan and Ottoman-era influences visible in pies, peppers, spiced dishes and bean dishes. Beans from the western lakes are especially well known.

name: Aegean islands
summary: The Cyclades, Dodecanese and nearby islands cook with what dry, windy, rocky land and sea provide: pulses, capers, tomatoes, octopus and local cheeses.

name: Epirus
summary: A mountainous north-western region famous for hand-rolled pies with greens and cheese, and for sheep and goat dairy and meat.

name: Mexico City and central Mexico
summary: The capital and its surroundings, where food from every state meets. Street food such as tacos al pastor, tamales and esquites is part of daily life, alongside markets, fondas and old traditions of maize cooking.

name: New England
summary: The north-eastern coast, with a long fishing tradition and a cooking shaped by British settlers. Clams, cod, lobster, dairy, maple and apples are its backbone, and chowder and baked pies are at the heart of the regional table.

name: The South and Texas
summary: A region of fried, smoked and slow-cooked food, with strong African American, Native American and European roots. Pork, chicken, cornmeal, buttermilk and greens are everyday foods, and Texas adds beef barbecue and a border cuisine of its own.

name: Louisiana
summary: South Louisiana has Creole cooking from New Orleans and the rural Cajun cooking of the bayous. French, Spanish, West African and Native American traditions blend in rice dishes, gumbos and seafood, all built on the onion, celery and bell pepper trio.

name: Midwest
summary: The central farm belt of dairy, grain and livestock. German, Scandinavian and Eastern European settlers shaped hearty foods such as cheese, sausages and baked goods, and Wisconsin in particular is known for its cheese and curds.

name: West Coast
summary: The Pacific states, with a strong emphasis on fresh seasonal produce, seafood and wild salmon, a Native American heritage and Asian and Mexican influence. San Francisco is known for sourdough bread, and the Pacific Northwest for salmon cooked on cedar.

name: Quebec
summary: A province with a French-Canadian food culture that is distinct from the rest of the country. Maple syrup, pork, cheese curds, rich winter dishes and pastry are common, with celebrated festive meals such as the réveillon and the sugar shack feast in spring.

name: Atlantic Canada
summary: The Maritime provinces and Newfoundland and Labrador, where cooking is shaped by the Atlantic, by British and Irish settlers and by Acadian and Indigenous traditions. Preserved fish and meat, root vegetables, seafood and boiled dinners are typical.

name: Ontario
summary: Canada's most populous province, with orchards, dairy farms and a large immigrant population. Traditional baking such as butter tarts and the cooking of its many communities sit side by side.

name: The Prairies
summary: Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, the grain-growing and cattle-raising heartland. Ukrainian, Polish, German and Icelandic settlers left a legacy of dumplings, sausages, breads and preserves.

name: British Columbia
summary: The Pacific province, with mild-climate farms and an ocean coast. Salmon and shellfish, berries and a strong Chinese, Japanese and South Asian food culture shape the cooking, along with the many Indigenous nations of the coast.

name: Havana and the West
summary: The capital and the tobacco-growing west. Roast pork with garlic and sour-orange mojo, boiled root vegetables and black beans with rice are everyday and festive staples.

name: Central Cuba
summary: A region of cattle ranches, rice paddies and sugar cane. Beef dishes, rice and sweets made with cane sugar feature strongly in home cooking.

name: Oriente (East)
summary: The east, around Santiago de Cuba and Baracoa, has the strongest Caribbean and Haitian links. Coconut and cacao are important around Baracoa, and rice is often cooked together with red beans.

name: Portland and the Blue Mountain foothills
summary: The wet north-eastern parish around Port Antonio is the best-known home of jerk, a smoke-and-spice barbecue tradition associated with the Maroon communities of the hills. Allspice, scotch bonnet and coconut are central.

name: St Elizabeth
summary: A farming parish in the south-west, often called the breadbasket of Jamaica, with cassava, vegetables and fresh river shrimp. Boiled spicy pepper shrimp are sold at roadside stalls in Middle Quarters.

name: Kingston
summary: The capital draws together the island's food cultures, from curries introduced by Indian migrants to pastry-and-spice patties and Chinese-Jamaican takeaways, alongside street food and Sunday rice dinners.

name: New South Wales
summary: Australia's most populous state, centred on Sydney. Harbour and coastal seafood, especially oysters, sits alongside a very diverse migrant restaurant scene and a long tradition of beef and wheat farming inland.

name: Victoria
summary: The south-eastern state around Melbourne, known for cafe culture and for the postwar influence of Greek and Italian migrants. Dairy farming and cool-climate produce supply much of the cooking.

name: Tropical North (Queensland and the Top End)
summary: The warm, wet north, where river and reef fish such as barramundi are staples and rainforest plants like lemon myrtle are used as flavourings. Tropical fruit and Asian-influenced cooking are common.

name: South Australia
summary: A dry southern state with a strong wine and olive-growing tradition. Adelaide has its own street-food customs, including the pie cart and the pie floater.

name: Tasmania
summary: The island state to the south, with cool maritime produce. It is known for farmed salmon, oysters, apples and cheeses. Lutruwita is the name used by Tasmanian Aboriginal people.

name: Northland
summary: The warm northern peninsula where Māori settlement is deep and long. Kūmara is the best-known crop, and shellfish and fish from the coast are widely eaten.

name: Hawke's Bay
summary: A sunny east-coast region of orchards, vineyards and sheep farms. Stone fruit, apples, lamb and wine are the local specialities.

name: Otago and Southland
summary: The cold deep south, famous for Bluff oysters from Foveaux Strait, hearty baking and regional favourites such as the Southland cheese roll.

name: Central Viti Levu
summary: Suva and the Rewa and Tailevu areas, with a large market culture. Dalo, cassava, and river and reef produce are staples, and lovo and kava remain central to village life.

name: Western Viti Levu
summary: The drier west around Nadi and Lautoka, the heart of the sugar-cane belt. Indo-Fijian cooking is especially strong here, with curries, dhal, roti and snacks sold in markets and shops.

name: Vanua Levu
summary: The second-largest island, quieter and more rural, with coconut plantations, farming communities and a mix of Fijian and Indo-Fijian households. Cassava, taro and coconut are common.

name: Lau Islands
summary: A scattered chain of small eastern islands, remote from the main islands and historically in close contact with Tonga. Coconut, root crops and fish dominate, and the food is simple and island-based.

name: Upolu
summary: The most populous Samoan island, home to the capital Apia. Village cooking follows the umu, taro, breadfruit and coconut pattern, while Apia's markets and shops supply produce, fish and baked goods to the wider island.

name: Savaiʻi
summary: The largest and more rural of the two main islands. Cooking here remains closely tied to village gardens, reef and lagoon fishing and the Sunday umu, with taro, breadfruit and green bananas as everyday staples.

name: Apia
summary: The capital and port on the north coast of Upolu. Markets, bakeries and tinned foods make it the place where imported and Chinese-influenced dishes such as sapasui and baked coconut buns are most visible next to traditional umu food.

name: Tongatapu
summary: The main island, with the capital Nuku'alofa and its central market. It is the main commercial and ceremonial centre, so feast food, pork, root crops and market produce from across the kingdom come together here.

name: Vavaʻu
summary: A northern island group of sheltered waters and many small islands. Fishing and seafood are prominent alongside garden crops, and the group is also known for growing vanilla.

name: Haʻapai
summary: A central group of low coral islands where life is quiet and largely subsistence-based. Reef fishing, coconut and root crops make up much of the diet.

name: ʻEua
summary: A raised, forested island with higher and wetter land than the rest of Tonga, known for its farming. Root crops, vegetables and fruit grown here are sent to markets elsewhere in the kingdom.

name: Bahia
summary: The North-Eastern state where the strongest West African influence on Brazilian cooking is found. Dende palm oil, coconut milk, fresh and dried shrimp, peppers and black-eyed peas define its food, which is also tied to Candomblé religious tradition.

name: Minas Gerais
summary: An inland, mountainous south-eastern state with a hearty farmhouse kitchen. Dairy and cheese, pork, beans, collard greens and cassava starch feature strongly, and many dishes come from the wood-stove cooking of rural homes.

name: Sao Paulo
summary: Brazil's most populous state, shaped by immigration from Italy, Japan, Lebanon and elsewhere. Its food is urban and cosmopolitan, with snack bars (lanchonetes) and bakeries selling fried and baked savoury snacks.

name: Rio Grande do Sul
summary: The southernmost state, part of the Pampas grassland shared with Uruguay and Argentina. Cattle-ranching gaucho culture gives it churrasco, plus German and Italian immigrant traditions.

name: Amazon (North)
summary: The northern rainforest and river region, where cooking draws mainly on indigenous knowledge. Bitter cassava and its by-products such as tucupi and tapioca gum, river fish and forest herbs like jambu are central.

name: Coast (Lima)
summary: The dry Pacific strip and its capital, Lima, which absorbed Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese cooks. Very fresh fish, limes and ají chillies feed ceviche and tiradito, while Chifa and Nikkei kitchens added soy sauce, wok cooking and sashimi technique.

name: Andes (Sierra)
summary: The highlands, where potatoes, maize, quinoa and fava beans were domesticated or long cultivated. Food is hearty, uses aromatic herbs such as huacatay, and includes the earth-oven feast pachamanca and the maize beer chicha de jora.

name: Amazon (Selva)
summary: The eastern jungle, where river fish, plantains, cassava and leaf-wrapped dishes dominate. Bijao and banana leaves are used to wrap and steam rice and meat.

name: Pampas and Buenos Aires
summary: The fertile plains around Buenos Aires, the centre of beef production and the largest Italian and Spanish settlement. Grilled beef and breaded cutlets sit beside pasta, pizza and pastries.

name: North-West (Andean)
summary: The provinces of Salta, Jujuy and Tucuman, with strong indigenous Andean food traditions. Corn, squash, beans, potatoes and chilli feature in stews, empanadas and husk-wrapped humitas.

name: Cuyo
summary: The Andean-foothill provinces of Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis. Irrigated vineyards and olive groves make it Argentina's wine heartland, and its cooking also uses goat, walnuts, dried fruit and tomatoes.

name: Patagonia
summary: The cold, windy southern plateau and Andean lakes, known for lamb roasted on iron crosses over embers, as well as trout, wild game and berry sweets.

name: Litoral and Mesopotamia
summary: The north-eastern region between the Parana and Uruguay rivers, with Guarani influence. River fish, cassava and corn are widely used, as in the cheese bread chipa.

name: Caribbean coast
summary: Hot, humid lowlands with African, indigenous and Spanish influences. Cooking uses coconut, fresh fish, cassava, plantain and salty fresh cheeses, with fried street snacks.

name: Andean highlands (Bogotá and Antioquia)
summary: The cool, mountainous heart of Colombia, including the Bogotá plateau and the paisa region of Antioquia. Potatoes, corn, beans, pork and chicken feature in thick soups and large plates.

name: Pacific coast
summary: A rainy, forested coastline with strong Afro-Colombian food traditions. Fish, shrimp, coconut and plantain dominate, with herbs and tropical fruit.

name: Llanos (Orinoquía)
summary: Eastern plains and cattle country shared with Venezuela. Open-fire beef, cassava, plantain and river fish are central to llanero cooking.

name: Central valley (Santiago)
summary: Chile's agricultural heartland, with a Mediterranean climate and the capital Santiago. Fresh corn, tomatoes, beef, empanadas and summer drinks are typical.

name: Northern Chile (Atacama and Altiplano)
summary: Desert and high Andean cuisine shaped by oasis farming, Aymara and Atacameño traditions and the nearby Pacific. Quinoa, potato, corn, llama meat and seafood are used.

name: Chiloé and the south
summary: A misty southern archipelago where potatoes (hundreds of native varieties), shellfish, smoked meats and wood-fired cooking define the diet.

name: Araucanía (Mapuche cuisine)
summary: The traditional lands of the Mapuche people. Wheat and corn (mote), beans, squash, apples and Araucaria pine nuts feature, along with smoked chilli (merkén).

name: West Coast
summary: A wet, remote strip on the South Island's west. It is known for the spring whitebait run and for wild foods gathered from forest and river.
